faqs.question: Is Halloween a public holiday in the UK?
faqs.answer: No. 31 October is an ordinary working and school day in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, so most celebrating happens after school, from about 17:00, and at weekend parties.

faqs.question: What is guising in Scotland?
faqs.answer: Guising is the Scottish forerunner of trick-or-treating. Guisers in masks visited neighbours, challenged them to guess who was underneath, and recited a rhyme, riddle or song before accepting a scone or other food.

faqs.question: Why did people in Scotland and Ireland carve turnips instead of pumpkins?
faqs.answer: Turnips were what grew there. A smouldering peat ember or a candle went inside, and Celtic Studies lecturer Pamela O'Neill calls this the likely origin of pumpkin carving, which took over after emigrants reached North America.

faqs.question: What is Nos Galan Gaeaf?
faqs.answer: It is the Welsh name for Halloween night, meaning the night of the winter calends; Calan Gaeaf itself is 1 November. You will also see it written Nos Calan Gaeaf, but Galan is the mutated form used after Nos.

faqs.question: How much do people in Britain spend on Halloween?
faqs.answer: Not much. A YouGov survey of 2,069 GB adults in September 2025 found 55% of those who celebrate spend under £25 and only 8% spend more than £100.

faqs.question: Why do some British people dislike Halloween?
faqs.answer: Mostly indifference, but some see it as American. In YouGov's 2024 poll, 10% of non-celebrators said it was an Americanism and 8% said it was too commercialised, and in 2025, 48% said it is not a GB tradition.

faqs.question: Do people in Northern Ireland set off fireworks at Halloween?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the fireworks calendar there is built around Halloween rather than 5 November. Northern Ireland requires a licence to buy, possess or use most fireworks, and display applications for Halloween close in mid-October.

faqs.question: What is barmbrack?
faqs.answer: Barmbrack is an Irish fruit loaf eaten at Halloween in Northern Ireland and Ireland. It is traditionally baked with a ring inside, and whoever finds the ring is said to be next to marry.

faqs.question: Do the clocks go back before Halloween in the UK?
faqs.answer: Yes. UK clocks go back on the last Sunday in October, which was 25 October in 2026 and falls on 31 October itself in 2027, so it is dark by early evening when trick-or-treating starts.

faqs.question: Is Halloween bigger than Bonfire Night in the UK?
faqs.answer: No. YouGov's 2024 poll found 44% of Britons prefer Bonfire Night on 5 November and only 16% prefer Halloween, although 18 to 24-year-olds lean towards Halloween.

# How Is Halloween Celebrated in the UK? A Four-Nation Guide

How is Halloween celebrated in the UK? Quietly, next to the American version. In a [YouGov poll of 2,069 British adults in September 2025](https://yougov.com/en-gb/articles/53067-uk-halloween-spending-shopping-trends-2025), 51% said they do not celebrate it at all, and the most common activities were handing out sweets to trick-or-treaters (28%), watching Halloween films (24%) and carving pumpkins (22%).

The four nations also reach 31 October from different directions: Scottish guising, the Welsh Nos Galan Gaeaf, Northern Ireland's licensed fireworks, and an England where Bonfire Night on 5 November still wins. If you are sending a greeting to family there, two platform-wide SubhSandesh numbers apply: 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone, and each page averages 11.1 views. Neither figure is Halloween-specific.

Below: the nations side by side, what historians actually support about Samhain, the Americanisation argument, and how Halloween sits next to Bonfire Night.

## What does Halloween in the UK look like today?

Halloween in Britain is a minority, low-spend, last-minute event. The same YouGov survey found 55% of people who mark it spend less than £25, only 8% spend more than £100, and 57% of celebrators start planning just a week before.

It skews young. Dressing up is a 16% activity overall but 37% among 18 to 24-year-olds. YouGov samples Great Britain, so Northern Ireland is not in these figures.

Trick-or-treating happens in a narrow window after dark. A [peer-reviewed study of the UK STATS19 road-crash database (Hsu et al., 2021)](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC8430693) covered 73,587 child casualties from 1990 to 2017. It found more child casualties between 17:00 and 19:00 on Halloween than on other holidays or ordinary days, and a 34.2% higher risk of being killed or seriously injured between 17:00 and 18:00. Reflective strips are worth adding.

## How do England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland celebrate Halloween differently?

One date, four back-stories. Each nation follows the same order: name, lantern, signature custom, today.

### England: All Hallows' Eve, overshadowed by 5 November

**Name:** Halloween, short for All Hallows' Eve, the night before All Saints' Day on 1 November. **Lantern:** the pumpkin, carved by 22% of British adults according to YouGov. **Signature custom:** none survives strongly; England's big autumn fire night is Bonfire Night, five days later. **Today:** sweets at the door, parties for the under-25s, then fireworks on 5 November.

### Scotland: guising and neep lanterns

**Name:** Hallowe'en, or Oidhche Shamhna in Scottish Gaelic. A Gaelic saying quoted by Celtic Studies lecturer [Pamela O'Neill (University of Sydney, October 2025)](https://theconversation.com/samhain-the-true-non-american-origins-of-halloween-266582) translates as "on Samhain night, calves become stirks", which ties the night to the farming year. **Lantern:** a turnip, the Scots neep, with a smouldering peat ember or a candle inside. O'Neill calls this the likely origin of pumpkin carving.

**Signature custom:** guising. Guisers challenged neighbours to guess who was under the mask, then recited a rhyme, riddle or song before accepting a scone. On South Uist the masks were painted sheepskin, sometimes with a sheep's skull. **Today:** the doorstep visit keeps the same shape: a costume, a knock, something given in return.

### Wales: Nos Galan Gaeaf and the tail-less black sow

**Name:** Nos Galan Gaeaf, the "night of the winter calends". Calan Gaeaf itself is 1 November, and calan is a Latin loan word from calends, according to Aberystwyth Celtic Studies lecturer [Simon Rodway (October 2023)](https://theconversation.com/nos-galan-gaeaf-the-traditional-welsh-celebration-being-eclipsed-by-modern-halloween-210939). **Lantern:** none in his account; the light was the bonfire, the coelcerth.

**Signature custom:** in south Wales young people went door to door like trick-or-treaters. In Powys the gwrachod, men in sheepskins and masks, drank heavily and demanded gifts. Walking home from the fire meant risking the Hwch Ddu Gwta (tail-less black sow) and the headless Ladi Wen. **Today:** posters translate Halloween as Nos Galan Gaeaf, and children trick-or-treat as elsewhere.

### Northern Ireland: fireworks and barmbrack

**Name:** Halloween, or Oíche Shamhna in Irish. **Lantern:** historically the turnip, the Gaelic tradition O'Neill describes. **Signature custom:** fireworks. Northern Ireland requires a licence to buy, possess or use most fireworks, and [nidirect's fireworks page](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/fireworks) sets a mid-October closing date for Halloween display applications (16 October in 2026). **Food:** barmbrack, a fruit loaf traditionally baked with a ring inside. **Today:** Halloween firework displays alongside trick-or-treating.

### The four nations compared

This table puts the four nations side by side on the same five points.

| Nation | Traditional name | Lantern vegetable | Signature food or custom | Modern practice |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| England | All Hallows' Eve | Pumpkin (modern) | Bonfire Night on 5 Nov takes the bonfire role | Sweets at the door; 22% of GB adults carve pumpkins |
| Scotland | Oidhche Shamhna (Gaelic) | Neep (turnip) lit with an ember or candle | Guising: a rhyme, riddle or song for a scone | Costumed doorstep visits |
| Wales | Nos Galan Gaeaf | None recorded; coelcerth bonfire | Gwrachod in Powys; Hwch Ddu Gwta tales | Posters say Nos Galan Gaeaf; trick-or-treat |
| Northern Ireland | Oíche Shamhna (Irish) | Turnip (Irish tradition) | Barmbrack; licensed fireworks | Halloween display licences close mid-October |

Scotland and Wales have the deepest documented customs; England's 31 October looks most imported because its fire night is 5 November.

## Did Halloween really come from Samhain? What historians support

Partly. The name and date are Christian, and the "ancient Celtic new year" story is far weaker than most Halloween pages suggest.

**Well supported:** Rodway traces Halloween to AD 609 or 610, when Pope Boniface IV dedicated the Pantheon to Mary and all the martyrs. The feast was fixed on 1 November in the eighth century and extended to the whole church by Gregory IV in the ninth. All Hallows' Day gave its eve the name.

**Also supported:** Gaelic-speaking Ireland, Gaelic Scotland and the Isle of Man kept a festival called Samhain at this time of year, presented in early medieval Irish literature as a time of uncanny events and otherworldly visits.

**Not supported:** Samhain as a pan-Celtic festival. Rodway finds no evidence it was celebrated in Wales, and says the claim that it marked the Celtic new year rests on "the speculation of comparative mythologists". O'Neill notes the Samhain activities we know of are recorded from the early 18th century, so druids in animal skins on 31 October are not documented practice.

Two notes. Historian Ronald Hutton's *The Stations of the Sun* (Oxford University Press, 1996) has a chapter on Samhain, but it is not open access, so this page relies on the two Celtic Studies lecturers instead. And O'Neill calls 1 November All Souls' Day; it is All Saints' Day, with All Souls' on 2 November.

## Is Halloween an American import in the UK?

It is a returned export. YouGov's 2025 survey found 48% of British adults say Halloween is "not a GB tradition", and 81% feel it is more commercialised than ten years ago. In [YouGov's October 2024 poll](https://yougov.com/en-gb/articles/50833-how-do-britons-feel-about-halloween), 10% of people not celebrating gave "an Americanism" as their main reason, and another 8% said it was too commercialised.

The customs went west first. O'Neill points to the Highland Clearances and the Great Irish Famine, which moved much of rural Scotland and Ireland to North America, where people reproduced the rituals of home. The turnip became a pumpkin, and guising became trick-or-treating.

The usual claim is that American-style trick-or-treating spread through Britain from the 1980s. We could not find an open source that measures it, so treat that date as received wisdom. Rodway records the "common complaint" in Wales that local customs have been "eclipsed by an increasingly homogenised and commercialised event imported from the USA".

## Halloween vs Bonfire Night: which do Britons prefer?

Bonfire Night, by a wide margin. YouGov's 2024 poll found 44% of Britons prefer Guy Fawkes Night and only 16% prefer Halloween, while 21% like neither and 15% like both equally. Younger people lean the other way: 21% of 18 to 24-year-olds prefer Halloween, against 7% of over-65s.

Bonfire Night marks the foiled Gunpowder Plot of 5 November 1605, five days after Halloween: Saturday 31 October and Thursday 5 November in 2026, Sunday and Friday in 2027.

They do different jobs. Halloween is a doorstep night for children, while Bonfire Night is a public display night; Northern Ireland flips that, with licensed displays built around Halloween. The same poll found 49% of Britons put the upper age for trick-or-treating at 15 or younger.

## How to send a Halloween greeting to family in the UK

If your grandparents are in Cardiff or your cousins in Glasgow, the [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) has a family mode. You add a letter, up to six photos and a word to carve on the pumpkin. They knock three times on a little haunted house, carve the jack-o'-lantern until your word glows, and read your letter by flashlight.

In family mode the closing question becomes "Will you be my favourite little pumpkin?". The Kids tone has no blood, no gore and no jump scares. It ends with a 1080×1920 Boo License marked "Valid every 31 October, forever", and you get an email the first time they answer. It opens in any phone or laptop browser, with no app or account.

Timing matters less than people fear. Our nearest measured analogue is Raksha Bandhan 2026 (n=89 pages, not Halloween data), where 49.4% of pages were built on the festival day itself and the median lead time was 0 days. A page made on the afternoon of 31 October is normal.

For a grandparent who would rather hear you than read you, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a voice note of up to 60 seconds and up to 12 photos. For family and kids, its No button never appears.

## When a Halloween web page is the wrong choice

Often, in Britain. With 66% of Britons not marking Halloween in 2024, an older relative who regards it as an Americanism may find a pumpkin-themed link baffling. A Bonfire Night text may land better.

Someone with no smartphone or browser habit is better served by a card through the letterbox, and the interface is English only, which matters for a Welsh-speaking grandparent.

Both pages are one-person greetings, not party invitations or a way to organise a guising group. And if you are in the same kitchen, a slice of barmbrack beats any link.
